claims.text: An answer about a default carries no sign of having been checked, so an invented one can be worded as confidently as a correct one; the wording cannot reliably tell them apart, but the official page for your version can.
At stage-0 docs/craft/ai-prompt-examples.md is a Vietnamese page holding, in order, a bad question, a good question, three tasks to hand over, three to keep back, and a closing paragraph.
claims.source_hint: examples/don-hang at stage-0: docs/craft/ai-prompt-examples.md, its H2 headings (lines 3, 11, 19, 27, 34)

claims.text: The bad-question example in that file is the single sentence 'Viết cho tôi chức năng hủy đơn hàng', and the file gives its cost as code that looks reasonable, uses a library you do not have, and follows conventions that are not the team's.

The good-question example in the same file attaches the code (OrderService.Cancel, the method that cancels an order, marked '(dán code)'), the versions (.NET 10, PostgreSQL 17), the rule, the current wrong behaviour, one constraint, and asks why and what in .NET causes the bug.

The versions named in that file, .NET 10 and PostgreSQL 17, are the versions pinned in content/versions.yaml for dotnet and postgresql; PostgreSQL is the database the project stores its orders in (db/seed.sql).

The same file's 'Ba việc nên giao' lists exactly three: explaining unfamiliar code, generating test cases (listing edge cases for a method), and rubber-ducking (writing the problem out for a machine to read, where you often see the bug yourself).

The same file's 'Ba việc không nên giao' lists exactly three: questions about default values, limits and versions; code you have not read line by line; and real customer data, which must not be pasted into any outside tool.

The same file states as its reason for sending version and default questions to the documentation that the assistant produces text that sounds reasonable, not verified truth ('không phải sự thật đã kiểm chứng').

The same file's closing paragraph compares the assistant to a very confident, broadly informed colleague who is sometimes completely wrong in the same voice used when right, and prescribes treating its output as that colleague's draft: read, check, then use.
The same file states 'Bạn ký tên vào commit, không phải nó' — the commit carries your name, not the assistant's.

A prompt carrying five parts — code, versions in force, the rule that must hold, what happens instead, one constraint — yields an answer you can judge; three words and a file do not. An answer you cannot judge saves less work than it seems to.

A reply that carries no new information, such as 'still wrong', gives the assistant nothing new to work from, so the next version is likely to be another guess; the step that helps is a changed prompt.

Asking for the reasoning and for a place in the documentation gives the answer its own handle for checking; the page it points at is part of the draft too, so confirm it is the official one for your version.

Work worth handing over is work whose result you can check cheaply: a run, a list you only read and prune, or a written-out failure whose pointed-at line the failing sample confirms or refutes. The lesson adds repetitive code a single run settles, beyond the page's three.

Writing the failure out as a prompt for the assistant often shows you the bug before any answer arrives, so it is worth doing even unsent; the lesson attributes this to the file's 'Vịt cao su' item, which says you frequently see the error yourself.
A confident tone is not evidence that anything was checked: a wrong answer and a correct one arrive worded alike, which is why an apology followed by an equally certain second version is the symptom.

When a draft holds, read every line before it enters a commit; your name is on it, and on teams that review before merge someone reads the change and asks why each line is there. Later readers ask why code is written that way.

Nothing in the situation's prompt said which project it was for, and what came back showed it: a naming style this repository does not use and a helper method it does not have. Stated as what the answer showed, not as the cause of it.
The page's bad question has the same shape as the situation's prompt — a line of intent and nothing else — but a different subject: it asks for an order-cancel feature, not a fix to a wrong total.
A boundary case is an input at the edge of what a method accepts.

claims.text: Real customer data is kept out of outside tools because of disclosure, not because an answer would be hard to check. The other two kept-back items carry their own stated reasons: unverified text for defaults, limits and versions, and your name on the commit for code you have not read.
A test is a small run that calls your code on chosen inputs and checks what comes back (broad enough to cover unit and integration tests).
A colleague tells you when a question makes no sense; an assistant may answer it anyway.
